chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from Sa'id ibn Yasar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who gave money to another man and said, 'I am giving it to you to be a reserve for my two daughters, so-and-so and so-and-so.' Then the old man, after giving the money, decided to take back twenty-five hundred dinars from him and bought a female slave for his grandson with it. Then the old man died, and a dispute arose between the two female slaves and the boy, or one of them. She said, 'Woe to you, by Allah, you are marrying your female slave unlawfully. Our father bought her for you from our money that he gave to so-and-so, and he bought this female slave for you from it. So you are marrying her unlawfully; she is not permissible for you.' The young man refrained from the female slave. He asked, 'What do you think about that?' He (the Imam) said, 'Is not the man who gave the money the father of the two female slaves, and he is the grandfather of the boy, and he bought the female slave for him?' I said, 'Yes.' He said to him, 'Let him approach his female slave, if the grandfather is the one who gave it and he is the one who took it back.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a deposit used by the agent for a different purchase for a third party?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal status of a female slave purchased with deposited funds, ruling that the grandson’s marriage to her is permissible because the grandfather, as the original owner of the wealth, effectively retained the right of disposal. It highlights the Shia juristic principle that the donor’s intent and continued ownership of the principal sum validate the agent’s subsequent acquisition for a third party, preventing claims of invalidity based on the source of funds. The ruling underscores the importance of tracing the chain of ownership in *mudarabah*-like arrangements to determine marital eligibility (*mahram* status).
